---
title: "Disrupt-Potentiate-Rewire-Homeostasis (DPRH)"
author: "Anselm Jeong"
date: "2026-01-26"
bibliography: "Metaplasticity.bib"
---

Drawing on insights gained from psychedelics, we can now propose a model that can integrate various NPETs into a single model. We have seen that psychedelics first induce widespread network desynchronization to create a state of "chaos," followed by an enhanced neuroplastic window that enables network reconfiguration or the remodeling of the attractor landscape.

This motif can be applied to ECT with some modification. ECT induces controlled seizures that trigger extensive neurophysiological changes [@Deng2024]. Unlike pharmacological interventions that gradually modulate synaptic function, ECT causes an abrupt and massive disruption of brain activity. Also, the following period of extensive network changes overlaps with that of significantly increased neuroplasticity. Furthermore, just as psychedelic therapy requires subsequent psychotherapy, the effects of ECT are often difficult to sustain without maintenance pharmacotherapy.

The disrupt-potentiate-rewire (DPR) model by Ousdal et al. [@ousdalEtAl2022] was originally proposed to account for the neurobiological effects of ECT; however, this model naturally aligns with rapid-onset antidepressants and can also be applied to traditional antidepressants. In summary, when sufficient energy is applied to disrupt existing network configurations while simultaneously enhancing neuroplasticity, the subsequent, more refined and gentle process of rewiring restores a healthy network configuration. The elegance of this model lies in its sequential logic: disruption breaks down barriers, potentiation provides the machinery, and rewiring actualizes the transformation. However, it must be remembered that this sequence is a double-edged sword, as it can lead to either therapeutic recovery or chaotic maladaptation [@ousdalEtAl2022]. Even the role of BDNF proved to be context-dependent, could be either neuroprotective or neurotoxic depending on the isoform (pro-BDNF vs. mature BDNF) and the receptor subtype (TrkB vs. p75NTR) involved [@dwivedi2009]. Thus, it would be safer to say that ECT and psychedelics act as controlled biological stressors that initiate the recovery process.

This perspective resonates with the "iPlasticity" (induced plasticity) proposed by Eero Castrén and colleagues to explain the mechanism of action of antidepressants [@castrén2017; @umemori2018]. He argued that antidepressants do not merely correct a chemical imbalance but rather reopen a flexible "critical period." In this model, medications provide an opportunity for change, while the rewiring is determined by subsequent environmental input and psychotherapeutic intervention. Given the clear similarities between the iPlasticity and DPR model, it seems evident that traditional antidepressants can also be integrated into the DPR framework.

In this paper, we seek to apply the DPR model to all NPETs. However, we also propose that an additional stage is required to sustain remission and prevent relapse. A prolonged state of heightened plasticity inherently carries the risk of reverting to previous maladaptive patterns. Since therapeutic interventions cannot be maintained indefinitely, the brain must eventually regain the intrinsic capacity to stabilize a healthy network organization. One candidate for this regulatory capacity is homeostatic plasticity. It governs the brain's plastic potential, determining when to permit reconfiguration and when to prioritize stability by resisting further alteration. 

There is growing evidence that this processe plays a key role in recovery from neuronal denervation, degeneration (10.1073/pnas.1213677110;10.3389/fnmol.2023.1148219), or during visual system plasticity (@10.1038/nrn1327). Recent studies have suggested that distinct phases of sleep may activate similar mechanisms to maintain neuronal network stability (10.1126/science.aah5982; 10.1038/ncomms12455). While the specific treatments that effectively target homeostatic mechanisms remain to be fully elucidated, we argue that regaining this capacity is essential for long-term recovery. Consequently, we modify the framework of Ousdal et al.[@ousdalEtAl2022] by appending a final stage, resulting in the "Disrupt–Potentiate–Rewire–Homeostasis (DPRH)" model.

## Homeostasis

Metaplasticity, or "the plasticity of synaptic plasticity," represents a higher-order regulatory mechanism that modulates the magnitude, threshold, and direction of synaptic changes [@Abraham1996; @Abraham2008]. The nervous system is perpetually confronted with the "stability–plasticity dilemma." It must remain plastic enough to incorporate new information while maintaining the stability of existing networks. Metaplasticity serves as a critical homeostatic mechanism that resolves this dilemma by balancing stability and flexibility across diverse timescales.

Homeostatic plasticity is one of the mechanisms of metaplasticity, referring to the capacity of neurons and neural circuits to regulate their own excitability and synaptic strength relative to the overall activity of the network to maintain stability, thereby influencing the future potential for Hebbian forms of plasticity [@Li2019a]. This conceptualization of homeostatic plasticity resonates with the definition of resilience proposed by Scheffer et al.[@schefferEtAl2024a] within the dynamical systems theory. In his review[@schefferEtAl2024a], Scheffer defined dynamical resilience as the capacity of a system to absorb perturbations without transitioning into alternative pathological attractors. The healthy mental state possesses a basin of attraction whose depth reflects resilience. In a resilient basin, the system can easily return to equilibrium despite transient disturbances. As this basin loses resilience, the risk increases that minor stressors can precipitate a transition into disordered states.

Homeostatic plasticity encompasses a suite of compensatory mechanisms, including synaptic scaling, intrinsic excitability adjustments, and metaplastic modulation of synaptic weights [@Turrigiano2004; @LeRoux2006; @Turrigiano2008; @Siddoway2014]. These implement feedback control loops that counteract deviations from set-point activity levels. When a neural circuit experiences sustained increases in excitatory drive, homeostatic downscaling of excitatory synapses and/or upregulation of inhibitory transmission restores balance. Conversely, prolonged suppression of activity triggers compensatory strengthening of excitatory connections or reduction of inhibitory drive [@Turrigiano1998].

The metaphorical equivalence becomes apparent when we assumed that that homeostatic plasticity provides the feedback mechanisms necessary to maintain the basin of attraction. Just as dynamical resilience reflects the capacity to return to baseline, homeostatic plasticity represents the neurobiological machinery that ensures a return to the functional set-point. Extending the concept to the psychological domain, high resilience implies the ability to withstand stressors and rapidly return to mental equilibrium.

### Empirical Evidence of Homeostatic Plasticity

Empirical evidence suggests that homeostatic plasticity at the circuit level mediates stress resilience at the behavioral level. Research on mesolimbic dopamine circuits has shown that homeostatic adaptations following chronic social stress distinguish resilient from susceptible animals [@Krishnan2007; @Isingrini2016]. Specifically, animals exhibiting behavioral resilience demonstrate compensatory synaptic adjustments in ventral tegmental area dopamine neurons that normalize circuit excitability despite ongoing stress exposure [@Friedman2014]. BDNF is also implicated in these mechanisms. Animals with enhanced BDNF signaling exhibit greater capacity for homeostatic synaptic adjustments and correspondingly greater behavioral resilience to chronic stress [@Taliaz2011; @Leschik2022].

The concept of "homeostatic disruption or failure" is relevant in understanding depression [@Naisberg1996;@Wang2025;@Andreescu2019]. Prolonged or severe perturbations can exhaust homeostatic mechanisms, leading to paradoxical or maladaptive compensatory responses [@Gou2025]. For instance, chronic stress can lead to excessive upregulation of inhibitory transmission in reward circuits, potentially contributing to anhedonia and motivational deficits. What began as a homeostatic response becomes pathological, contributing to the formation of a stable depressive attractor. This aligns with the dynamical systems concept of increasing "bad resilience"—the pathological state becomes increasingly resistant to interventions as maladaptive homeostatic adjustments entrench the disordered circuit configuration [@Christoffel2011; @Bath2017; @Pignatelli2021].

Building on this, Wang et al.[@wang2025] detailed how specific molecular deficits contribute to this homeostatic failure in depression. Altered expression of ion channels compromises intrinsic excitability, preventing neurons from maintaining a stable excitatory-inhibitory (E/I) set point. Furthermore, abnormalities in presynaptic neurotransmitter release, often influenced by glial signals such as TNF-α, impair the homeostatic regulation of network activity. These issues are compounded by deficits in synaptic scaling and signaling molecules, including retinoic acid pathways that modulate postsynaptic AMPA receptor density, which further undermine synaptic stability and entrench the pathological state [@arendt2015;@hu2020].

### Clinical implication of Homeostatic Plasticity

Several pharmacological agents show evidence of promoting homeostatic plasticity. Lithium has been shown to promote homeostatic downscaling of excitatory synaptic strength through effects on glycogen synthase kinase-3β (GSK-3β) signaling. This homeostatic adjustment may stabilize circuits prone to excessive excitability, thereby deepening the basin of attraction around euthymic states [@Salinas1999; @Gideons2017; @MachadoVieira2018; @Kavalali2020]. Valproate modulates GABAergic inhibition and can affect activity-dependent homeostatic plasticity in preclinical models [@Wang2012; @Zhang2003]. Its efficacy in preventing both manic and depressive episodes may reflect stabilization of circuits prone to excessive excitability or hypoactivity through enhanced homeostatic regulation.

Novel compounds targeting metaplastic mechanisms may offer more direct approaches to enhancing homeostatic plasticity. For example, drugs modulating metabotropic glutamate receptors (particularly mGluR2/3 and mGluR5) can shift the threshold for synaptic plasticity induction and affect homeostatic scaling mechanisms [@Hu2010; @Lscher2010]. Similarly, agents affecting neurosteroid synthesis—which modulate GABAA receptor function and have rapid antidepressant effects—may act partly by restoring E-I balance through homeostatic mechanisms [@Diviccaro2022; @Cutler2023].
